planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens or divisions in fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; willow gentian tolerates more sun than most gentians where summers stay cool and moist, but appreciates afternoon shade anywhere summers run hot.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade, siting the arching stems where they can lean over a path edge or companion planting without staking. Willow gentian earns its name from the long, gracefully arching stems clothed in paired, willow-like leaves, with sapphire-blue trumpet flowers clustered in the upper leaf axils from late summer into fall — a season when true blue is scarce in the shade garden. It is among the easiest gentians to grow in ordinary garden conditions, needing only consistent moisture and cool root run rather than the exacting scree conditions many alpine gentians demand. Established clumps slowly widen into an impressive fountain of foliage and late bloom; avoid dividing except to propagate, since plants resent disturbance and take a season or two to recover.

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall and leave exposed to winter cold for stratification, or plant container-grown divisions in spring, into humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; where summers run hot and dry, site in partial shade instead to keep the roots cool and moist.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, giving full sun in cool climates but shifting to partial shade wherever summers turn hot and dry. Crested gentian forms a low, spreading mound of narrow, glossy leaves topped from midsummer into early fall with clusters of up to eight upward-facing, deep-blue trumpet flowers, each throat striped with paler blue-green markings that give the species its 'crested' common name. It is one of the more forgiving gentians for the general perennial or rock garden border rather than a dedicated alpine scree bed, tolerating ordinary garden soil as long as drainage is adequate and moisture is steady through summer. Divide congested clumps in spring or fall to maintain vigor, and mulch lightly over winter in the coldest end of its range.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in evenly moist, well-drained, average to humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; in regions with hot, humid summers, site where the plant gets protection from intense afternoon sun.

directions: Plant in evenly moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, sheltering from harsh afternoon sun where summers run hot and humid. True Blue is a hybrid gentian bred from Gentiana makinoi and Gentiana scabra lines, producing upright, well-branched stems clothed in glossy foliage and topped from midsummer into early fall with an unusually long succession of large, pure blue, upward-facing trumpet flowers — a saturated, true blue that is rare among garden perennials blooming so late in the season. Unlike many gentians that sulk in ordinary garden soil, True Blue was selected for garden adaptability and performs reliably in a well-drained perennial border rather than demanding a dedicated scree or alpine bed. Established clumps increase steadily; divide only occasionally, since the plant resents frequent disturbance and takes a season to settle back in after division.
scientific_name_note: Hybrid gentian (Gentiana makinoi x Gentiana scabra); PP20433, introduced by Darrell Probst in 2008.

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant in fall for winter establishment and spring bloom in mild climates, or in early spring further north, in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Blue Ball's dense, compact habit makes tight spacing effective for a solid carpet of bloom.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun, avoiding intense afternoon heat wherever possible. Blue Ball is a distinctly compact selection of woodland forget-me-not, forming tidy, rounded mounds barely 6 inches tall that are smothered in dense clusters of the classic small, five-petaled, bright blue flowers with tiny yellow eyes in spring. Its neat, ball-shaped habit — considerably tighter and lower than the sprawling species — suits formal edging, container plantings, and underplanting spring bulbs where a looser forget-me-not would flop. It self-seeds readily once established, and an RHS Award of Garden Merit reflects its reliable garden performance. Shear lightly after the main flush to tidy the mounds if seed set is not wanted.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Winter Annual Flowers

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant in fall for winter establishment and spring bloom in mild climates, or in early spring further north, in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; part of the award-winning Sylva series bred for early, uniform flowering.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Rosylva breaks from the familiar blue of the species with clusters of bubble-gum pink flowers, each with a small yellow eye and pale midribs, covering low, mounding plants in spring and early summer. A Fleuroselect Gold Medal winner from the Sylva breeding series, it was selected for its early, abundant flowering and uniform habit, making it dependable for mass plantings, containers, and edging where a consistent pink carpet is wanted rather than the variable seedling color of open-pollinated strains. Combine with the blue-flowered species or 'Blue Ball' for a two-tone spring carpet under deciduous shrubs and around spring bulbs.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant small divisions or container-grown specimens in early fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; like other Corydalis flexuosa selections, Pere David goes dormant in summer heat, so mark its spot and interplant with later-emerging companions.

directions: Plant small divisions in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Pere David is a compact selection of Chinese blue corydalis, producing finely cut, blue-green ferny foliage low to the ground and a long spring display of slender, tubular, clear sky-blue flowers on short stems held just above the leaves. It stays noticeably tighter and lower-growing than the straight species or 'Blue Panda', making it well suited to the front of a shaded border, trough, or rock garden pocket where a taller selection would overwhelm the setting. Like its siblings, it vanishes into summer dormancy once heat arrives and re-emerges reliably from below ground the following late winter; interplant with hostas or ferns to fill the gap it leaves behind.

planting.note: Plant small divisions or container-grown specimens in early fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; this woodland species from Mount Omei in south-central China dislikes drought and is often semi-dormant to fully dormant through summer heat.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade beneath deciduous trees or shrubs; Omei fumewort is an upright Chinese woodland corydalis with light green, two- to three-part lobed foliage and dense racemes of slender, purple-flushed blue flowers carried well above the leaves in late spring and early summer. It flowers over a longer stretch where summers stay cool and consistently moist, and it dislikes prolonged drought, so a mulched woodland setting with reliable moisture suits it best. In the mildest end of its hardiness range the foliage can persist through much of the year, while in cooler gardens it tends toward semi-dormancy in summer heat, returning reliably from the crown once temperatures moderate. Combine with ferns, hellebores, and hostas in a shaded border for an understated, long-blooming companion to the more flamboyant blue and yellow corydalis species.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade in spring; like the blue species, 'Alba' spreads by stolons and self-sows moderately in suitable shaded, cool conditions.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade; 'Alba' is the pure white-flowered form of blue-eyed Mary, spreading by stolons into a low, loose mat of heart-shaped, bright green leaves dotted in early spring with clean white flowers in place of the species' vivid blue. It combines readily with the blue-flowered species, with yellow-flowered Epimedium, or with spring bulbs, brightening shaded corners where the straight species' saturated blue might otherwise dominate. Growth and vigor match the species closely — steady, well-behaved spread by runners and light self-seeding rather than aggressive colonization — so established clumps can simply be divided every few years to propagate more without special care.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database
